props.title: Seven habits of a secure pipeline

items.d: permissions: contents: read — grant writes per job
Short-lived cloud credentials, nothing to leak
Keep actions updated; scan workflows too

captions: Part eight. Security.

Your pipeline holds secrets and can push to
production.
That makes it a target.

Every job gets an automatic credential: the
GITHUB_TOKEN. It
lets the workflow call the GitHub API — comment
on a pull request, push a tag, publish a
package.
It expires when the job ends.
What it can do is set by the permissions
key.

Newer repositories default to read-only. Best
practice: start with
read, and grant write only for exactly what a
job needs.

Here: contents read, pull requests write, and
id-token write
for cloud login. Everything else, none.

If an attacker hijacks a step, least privilege
limits
the damage.
Now, that version after the at sign. A tag
like v4 is just a pointer, and its owner
can move it.

In March twenty twenty five, that's exactly what
happened.

Attackers compromised the popular tj-actions
changed-files action, and moved
its version tags to malicious code.

Tens of thousands of repositories used it. Their
workflows

pulled the bad code automatically, and some printed
secrets
into public logs.
Repositories pinned to a full commit hash were safe,
because a hash can't be moved.
So pin third-party actions to a commit hash, and
let Dependabot propose the updates.
The next trap is script injection.
Look at this step. It echoes the pull request
title, straight into a shell command.
But the title is written by whoever opened the

pull request. An attacker names their PR: quote,
semicolon,
curl evil dot sh, pipe to shell.

GitHub pastes that text into the script before
running
it. The shell sees a second command, and runs
it.

The fix: pass untrusted values through an
environment variable,
and quote it. Now the title is just data.
And be very careful with pull request target. It

runs with secrets, even for pull requests from
forks.
Here's the checklist.
One: set permissions to read by default.
Two: pin third-party actions to commit hashes.
Three: use OIDC instead of long-lived cloud keys.
Four: never paste untrusted input into run scripts.

Five: protect production with environments and
reviewers.

Six: keep self-hosted runners away from public
repos.

And seven: turn on Dependabot and code scanning,
which
can check your workflow files too.
